newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese cell phone operators discuss tie-up.
newsitem.headline: Japanese cell phone operators discuss tie-up.

text.p: Japanese cellular phone operators DDI Corp and IDO Corp said on Monday they are considering a partial alliance, but industry analysts said that serious obstacles stand in the way of a full merger.

The two companies said they are discussing cooperation in new digital cellular phone technology -- to go into operation in 1998 -- but the analysts said that Toyota Motor Corp's stake in the smaller phone operator IDO (Nippon Idou Tsushin Corp) would pose a barrier to full merger talks.
"It is very unlikely that the alliance would immediately develop into a full-scale merger, or expanded cooperation in other service areas," said Toshiaki Iba, analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.

"DDI won't initiate such talks unless Toyota withdraws from IDO's management," Iba said, adding DDI was worried about being involved with such a large company as Toyota, which tends to dominate its partners.

Long-distance carrier DDI said that its cellular phone affiliate, the Cellular Telephone Co group, was in talks with IDO about jointly introducing next-generation digital cellular phone services using cord division multiple-access technology, a digital format developed in the United States.
Industry sources said it was possible that DDI and IDO would move to build a nationwide network, providing common services and sharing equipment, to compete with industry titan NTT DoCoMo.
Despite higher tariffs than its rivals, NTT DoCoMo has more than half the Japanese cell phone market and is grabbing more on the strength of its name.

IDO, owned 27.2 percent by Toyota Motor, has been losing money, and with more mergers and acquisitions expected in the telecommunications sector, analysts are watching to see if cash-rich Toyota strengthens its role or withdraws.
Toyota already has stakes in two other Japanese telecom service companies -- long-distance carrier Teleway Japan Corp and international carrier International Digital Communications Inc.
But they are also losing money, and analysts such as Eric Gan of Goldman Sachs (Japan), say the best scenario for DDI would be to absorb all three companies Toyota has a stake in.
"That would make DDI a powerful conglomerate, but we don't know if it can happen," Gan said.

In the past several years, there has been speculation in the Tokyo stock market that DDI, 21.7 percent owned by chipmaker Kyocera Corp, may buy Teleway Japan, which owns nationwide fibre networks that complement DDI's networks.
But DDI and Toyota have denied the market talk, citing differences in corporate culture.
